implementation_notes: C has no lazy construct, so the classic structure is written by hand: a static pointer (or struct) for the value and a static pthread_once_t initialised with PTHREAD_ONCE_INIT, plus an accessor that calls pthread_once(&once, init_fn); the runtime guarantees the initialiser runs exactly once per process even when threads arrive together. This is the portable POSIX default; the initialiser cannot report failure through the interface, so the cell must encode it or the accessor must return a status.
pitfalls: pthread_once is process-wide per once_control and POSIX defines no way to reinitialise a flag: a per-object cell needs its own flag, and PTHREAD_ONCE_INIT only covers statically allocated flags, so per-object laziness is usually written with atomics or a mutex instead.

pthread_once gives no failure channel: if the initialiser fails, the flag is still done, so the accessor must expose the failure through the cell (NULL, errno or a status field) - an aborted process is the only alternative.
The initialiser runs while other threads block inside pthread_once, so it must not wait on those threads (classic deadlock: the initialiser joins a thread that calls the accessor).

variants.name: C11 call_once / once_flag
variants.implementation_notes: On a C11 toolchain <threads.h> provides call_once together with once_flag and ONCE_FLAG_INIT, the standard-track replacement for pthread_once; cppreference explicitly records pthread_once as the POSIX equivalent. Choose it when the program already requires C11 threads and you want to avoid a POSIX dependency, but check platform support first (embedded toolchains frequently ship pthread_once without threads.h).
pitfalls: C11 threads.h is the least portable part of C11: several embedded and older platforms implement pthreads but not call_once, so a build flag or fallback is usually required.
The function passed to call_once must return void and cannot signal failure, giving the same error-channel problem as pthread_once.

variants.name: Single-threaded null/sentinel guard
variants.implementation_notes: In code that is single-threaded by construction (event loop with no preemption, setup phase before threads start, signal-handler-free library initialisation) the whole pattern is a null or sentinel test plus one build call; the marker doubles as the error indicator. This is the historically classic form and remains correct only while the ordering argument holds - document the confinement, because adding one worker thread silently turns it into a data race.
pitfalls: It is a plain data race the moment a second thread can call the accessor: two builds, a torn pointer write, and no ordering guarantee for the object behind the pointer (use atomics or a once-primitive if that can ever happen).
A NULL marker cannot distinguish 'not built' from 'failed build', so a failing build is retried on every access unless a separate state field is added.
